weirdERC20Adjudication.question: Do 08-02 / 08-04 / 08-11 fall to the 'non-standard/weird ERC-20' known-invalid pattern?
weirdERC20Adjudication.governingPrinciple: The weird-ERC20 rule presupposes a protocol that integrates a FIXED, VETTED token set, and bars findings that import token variance the protocol never signed up for. PhlimboV3's promo slot is an ARBITRARY, OWNER-ONBOARDED partner token; the contract ships a bespoke non-reverting transfer helper whose stated purpose is surviving hostile token behaviour. Token variance is inside this protocol's threat model BY CONSTRUCTION, so the rule does not reach these findings by default. The protocol does constrain the set where it chose to (FoT/rebasing are rejected at PhlimboV3.sol:347/372) — and that guard is the proof that unguarded behaviours were NOT excluded by policy.

perFinding.08-02: NOT weird-ERC20. Blocklist/pause is USDT-class and USDT is the EXPLICIT exception to the rule. Three independent confirmations: (1) the team's own mock is commented 'USDT-style recipient blocklist' (Mocks.sol:98); (2) _tryTransfer exists solely to survive it; (3) the migrator NatSpec names 'a blocklisted address' as the anticipated case. A precondition the project mocks in its tests and names in its NatSpec is anticipated design, not unanticipated weirdness. VALID.
perFinding.08-04: Weird-ERC20-SHAPED but survives, on three independent grounds. (1) PRECEDENT: the identical defect is ledgered OPEN on the original (V3-L-02) — invalidating the byte-identical clone while the original stays open would be incoherent. (2) FRAMING: the core is a doc-vs-code deviation — story-025's NatSpec makes an UNCONDITIONAL claim ('never reverts', 'can never brick a pass') that the helper cannot honour. That falsification is a Law-2 defect and holds regardless of token realism. (3) INTENT-INTERNAL: _tryTransfer already handles the 0-byte return branch, so the author was demonstrably reasoning about non-standard returns and covered only part of the space. That is an incomplete implementation of the contract's own intent, not a complaint about exotic tokens. Token realism is retained as the SEVERITY anchor (why Low, not Medium), not as a validity bar. Concur with the sanitizer's rejection of this suppression. VALID.
perFinding.08-11: NOT weird-ERC20 at all — a codeless address is not an ERC-20, it is the absence of one. The defect is a missing existence check in a hand-rolled SafeERC20 substitute (precisely the check SafeERC20's isContract provides). Standard, legitimate audit finding. VALID.

law3Adjudications.surpriseTest: Would a competent, non-malicious owner calling finalizePromotion be SURPRISED that it confiscates stakers' earned promo? YES, decisively — and verified in source. Every artifact the owner would consult says the entitlement survives: PhlimboV3.sol:141-142 ('banked for out-of-band handling'), SolvencyDetermination.md:81 (counts it as a covered liability) and :99-100 ('the tokens never left, so the invariant is undisturbed'), and the sibling written in the SAME story wave gives blocked users a permissionless claimUnclaimable pull. Nothing anywhere warns that finalizing destroys. finalizePromotion presents as routine end-of-promotion housekeeping.
law3Adjudications.notRecklessAdmin: No owner malice is required or alleged, and the malicious framing is neither needed nor used. Surprise ⇒ footgun ⇒ in scope at honest severity.

law3Adjudications.surpriseTest: The base — emergencyTransfer drains tokens — is OBVIOUS and correctly Law-3-suppressed; it is not the finding. The surviving face is an ORDERING CONSTRAINT: return tokens first ⇒ full recovery (accumulator and debts intact); rotate first ⇒ irreversible silent destruction. An owner cannot derive that ordering from anything in the contract, AND the ledger entry itself currently advises the destructive order AS THE RECOVERY. An owner who follows the audit's own remediation advice destroys the entitlements. That is the maximum possible score on the surprise test.
law3Adjudications.mandatoryActionsEndorsed: The three mandatoryLedgerActions (strike 'recoverable, no fund loss'; invert the recovery advice; widen to the stable leg) are endorsed. Action 2 is the one that matters — leaving falsified recovery advice in the ledger is itself a Law-1 hazard.

law3Adjudications.surpriseTest: The owner CANNOT KNOW N is too large until the transaction fails — the consequence is non-obvious by construction. 'The owner should have chunked it' is unavailable as a rebuttal because seedUsers offers no chunking to choose. Not centralization, not a reckless-admin mistake.

Verified independently: MigratorV2V3.sol:64-68 documents it verbatim — sweeps 'INCLUDING amounts banked in unclaimable, leaving those claims unbacked... the accepted trade-off'. trapWarningValidity.question: Is a QA note whose purpose is warning against a plausible-but-harmful 'fix' valid output?
trapWarningValidity.verdict: VALID, and among the more valuable items in this run. Keep it.
reasoning: It is not a vulnerability claim, so no known-invalid pattern applies to it. The invalid list filters ASSERTIONS OF DEFECT; this asserts the opposite — that the code is correct and must not be 'corrected'.

Law 1 is affirmative here, not permissive. The trap warning PREVENTS an exploit: applying the obvious fix strands ~9.95 USDC per occurrence with no rescue function. Dropping the note for tidiness would leave a live landmine for the next reviewer. Law 1 requires keeping it.

Its danger profile is exactly what makes it worth writing down: `totalStaked-mutated-without-_updatePool` is a known-good discipline elsewhere in this codebase, so the future reviewer will be RIGHT about the pattern and WRONG about this instance. That is precisely the class of error a written warning catches and reasoning-from-first-principles does not.
KI-4 independently reinforces it: the omission is documented as by-design, so the obvious 'fix' would ALSO contradict the project's stated design. Two independent reasons not to apply it.
trapWarningValidity.requirement: The TRAP_WARNING block must survive into the QA bundle VERBATIM, as the classifier demands. It is the entry's entire reason for existing — a summarised or softened version does not do the job.
